name: Fatima Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Lambert & Sons, a family-run agency on the market square in a small town, the kind of place that's been there since the sixties. I'm in sales mostly, with a bit of lettings when someone's off. I start at half eight, ring round anyone who viewed at the weekend, then I'm out doing viewings and valuations, mostly older people selling the family home. I like knowing every street, which side gets the afternoon sun, which houses have damp. The paperwork wears me out, and so do buyers who ring at nine at night.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools in your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No, never. The office has something on the system that writes descriptions, but I write my own, the young lad uses it. I don't trust a thing that's never stood in the house to describe it. I'm not the best agent in the office, just steady, but my sellers like that I'm the same person every time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and I'd probably say it a bit too loudly in the office. People buy houses from people. Online I wouldn't say much, I don't really post about work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved. My job's fine, my pay's decent, and I've got my flat and about eight months put by. So nothing really changes for me, which is how I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on the same. I'd keep overpaying the mortgage on my flat by a hundred a month, like I do now. Maybe I'd let the young lad keep using his tool for descriptions, as long as I don't have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled. It's the picture where I don't have to think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about work that worries you even in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The market, more than anything. When rates go up, sales dry up and our commission drops, and that's nothing to do with AI. Last winter I had six weeks without a single completion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you get through those six weeks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Basic pay, the savings, and my boyfriend Hugo, who's an electrician, always has work. I didn't touch the savings in the end, but I watched the account a lot. It's why I like having the cushion.

say: I'd say **people buy houses** from people, so I'm not surprised.
I'd mostly keep quiet **online** about work.
think: I'd be **relieved** that my job and pay stay the same.
My **flat and savings** mean nothing changes for me.
do: Keep overpaying the **mortgage** by about £100 a month.
Let the young colleague use **his AI tool** while she writes her own.
S0.quote: When rates go up, sales dry up and our commission drops, and that's nothing to do with AI.
fieldNote: Her real worry is **interest rates**, not technology.
A **six-week drought** last winter taught her to value her cushion.
She is open about being **steady, not the best**.

steps.text: Keep overpaying the flat mortgage by about £100 a month
Carry on writing her own property descriptions by hand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a tool and the good agents will still be needed. At work I'd probably say I'll learn it when they make me. To friends I'd say it's the admin girls I feel sorry for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, the bits on that card are a lot of my day. Booking viewings, chasing solicitors, answering the website, writing up. If the office gets that done by a computer, they might decide they need fewer of us doing the viewings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what Lambert's actually bring in, and I'd learn it when I had to, not before. I'd put a bit more aside each month, maybe another hundred. And I'd keep my sellers close, because a seller who asks for me by name is the best job security I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's probably fine for a few years, but I don't like not knowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'the admin girls'. Who do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sandra and Bev in the back office. Sandra's been there twenty-two years and does every completion by hand. If the computer does completions, I don't know what Sandra does all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn it when you had to. What if the ones who learn it first are kept on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fair, and it's what Hugo says too. I suppose I'd go on whatever course they put on, but I wouldn't be first in the queue. I just don't like being told the old way is wrong when it works.

say: I'd say it's **a tool** and good agents will still be needed.
I'd tell friends I feel sorry for **the back office** staff.
think: A lot of my day, like **booking and chasing**, is on that card.
The office might decide it needs **fewer agents** for viewings.
do: Wait to see what **Lambert's** bring in before learning it.
Keep sellers close so they **ask for her** by name.
feel: She feels **uneasy** about **not knowing** what comes.
S1.quote: A seller who asks for me by name is the best job security I've got.
fieldNote: She admits **much of her day** is the desk work on the card.
She **resists learning** early, even when told early learners are kept.
Her worry for **Sandra** shows she sees the back office going first.

steps.text: Wait to see which system Lambert's buys before learning it
Add another £100 a month to savings
Ring past sellers every few months so they ask for her

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad and someone should stop it. At work I'd be asking Mr Lambert straight what it means for us. Online I'd still keep quiet, I think, but I'd be talking about nothing else at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm one of the first to go. I don't use the tools, I'm average, and I'm not the one who brings in the most instructions. If a computer can value, write, chase and haggle, the office needs one or two people for keys and viewings, and that won't be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd stop the extra mortgage payments and keep all the cash I can, so I've got closer to a year. I'd ask Hugo whether his firm could use someone on the phones and the quotes, because people still need electricians. Then I'd look at jobs where you have to be in the house, like inventory clerk, until the robots come around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Sick, a bit. But I've got the flat and the savings, so it's not the end of the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your job is part hands-on. Does the three years before robots help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but not much. Viewings are maybe a third of my week, and you don't need four of us for that. It's three years of a smaller job, if I'm lucky to keep one at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hugo that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, I think I'm finished at Lambert's, can I come and do your bookings? He'd laugh and then say yes. He's been asking me to help with his paperwork for two years.

say: I'd say it's **mad** and someone should stop it.
I'd ask **Mr Lambert** straight what it means for us.
think: I think I'm **one of the first** to go.
The office would need only **one or two people** for keys and viewings.
do: Stop extra mortgage payments to hold **a year of cash**.
Ask Hugo for work doing **phones and quotes** at his firm.
Look at **inventory clerk** jobs until the robots come.
feel: She feels **anxious**, a bit sick, but steadied by the **flat and savings**.
S2.quote: I don't use the tools, I'm average, and I'm not the one who brings in the most instructions.
fieldNote: She is **blunt** about why she'd be cut first.
Her fallback is **Hugo's electrical firm**, family rather than the state.
The **robot gap** feels like a smaller job, not a rescue.

steps.text: Stop overpaying the mortgage and hold a year of cash
Ask Hugo to take her on doing his firm's bookings and quotes
Apply for inventory clerk jobs that need someone in the house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years isn't long, but it's long enough not to panic. At work I'd still be asking what the plan is. To friends I'd say I'm looking around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's the same end as the fast one, just later. I'd have a couple of years to prove I'm worth keeping, or to get out on my own terms. I'm not sure which I'd pick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably go on the course when Lambert's put it on, because I'd rather not be the one who refused. I'd keep saving and pay less off the flat. And in a year or two I'd start helping Hugo on Saturdays, so I'm not starting from nothing if I need to move over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, still. Not as sick, but it's there in the background. I'd know where it was heading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go on the course this time. What changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough that refusing just looks stubborn. With two years' notice there's no point. With five, I'd look daft sitting it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know when to leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When they stop replacing people. If our back-office colleague Sandra retires and nobody takes her desk, that's the sign. I'd give it about six months after that.

say: I'd say five years isn't long, but it's **not panic time**.
I'd keep asking at work **what the plan is**, and tell friends I'm looking around.
think: It's **the same end** as the fast one, just later.
I'd have time to **prove my worth** or leave on my own terms.
do: Go on Lambert's **AI course** rather than refuse it.
Keep saving and **pay less** off the flat.
Start helping Hugo on **Saturdays** to have a fallback.
feel: She feels **anxious**, but with the worry **in the background**.
S3.quote: If our back-office colleague Sandra retires and nobody takes her desk, that's the sign.
fieldNote: The extra time makes her **willing to learn**, if only to avoid looking stubborn.
Her **warning sign** is an unfilled desk, not news headlines.
She hedges with **Saturday work** at her partner's firm.

steps.text: Sign up for the AI course when Lambert's runs it
Help with Hugo's electrical firm bookings on Saturdays
Keep building savings instead of overpaying the flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots can happen. At work I'd say let's see. To friends I'd say I'll be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be fine for most of it. I'd be 37 when it comes, which isn't old. I'd probably still be at Lambert's for a good few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, honestly. I'd keep paying down the flat so it's nearly clear by the time it lands. Maybe in five years or so I'd think about working with Hugo properly, depending on how things look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not really worried. It's far off, but it's coming. I'd rather not think about it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk that waiting means you leave it too late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, and Hugo would say so. But I've seen a lot of 'next big thing' come through the office and most of it didn't change much. I'd watch it, I just wouldn't jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would having the flat paid off mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means whatever happens, I've got a roof nobody can take. My mum always said own your four walls first. That's the one bit of advice I've actually followed.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a long time and lots can happen.
think: I'd likely stay at **Lambert's** for a good few years.
I'd be **37** when it comes, which isn't old.
do: Keep paying down **the flat** to near clear by then.
Think about working with **Hugo's firm** in about five years.
feel: She feels **uneasy** but not really worried, preferring **not to dwell**.
S4.quote: My mum always said own your four walls first. That's the one bit of advice I've actually followed.
fieldNote: With a decade, she returns to her **wait-and-see** instinct.
Her real security plan is **a paid-off flat**.
She's seen many **'next big things'** fizzle, which shapes her doubt.

steps.text: Keep overpaying the flat to clear it before 2036
Stay at Lambert's and review plans in about five years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, because I'd be out before I'd sorted anything. What would help is honest notice from the firm, like a year's warning, so I could move to Hugo's business properly. I don't want handouts, just time and a straight answer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the older sellers. A lot of my sellers are in their eighties and they want someone to sit with them and talk about their husband's garden. I don't think a computer does that, but I don't know if anyone will pay for it either.

headlineQuote: A lot of my sellers are in their eighties and they want someone to sit with them and talk about their husband's garden.
portrait: Fatima is a **27-year-old sales agent** at a family-run agency on a small-town market square.
She **never uses AI tools**, writes her own descriptions and trusts knowing every street.
Her cushion is **a flat** she's paying down and about eight months of savings.
In fast AGI she expects to be **cut first** and to fall back on her partner's electrical firm.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028**, when she'd be out before she'd sorted anything.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **a year's notice** and a straight answer from her firm, not handouts.
